articles.title: Los Boston Celtics apuestan fuerte por el 'lucense' Payton Pritchard con 44,2 millones más
articles.standfirst: 44,2 millones por dos años más para el base que lleva desde 2020 en Boston
articles.summary: 44,2 millones por dos años más para el base que lleva desde 2020 en Boston
articles.body: Payton Pritchard, base de los Boston Celtics, ha acordado una extensión de contrato por dos años y 44,2 millones de dólares, que incluye una opción mutua para la temporada 2029-30. "Imagina si hubiera escuchado a las personas que decían que no podía", comentó el 'lucense' Payton Pritchard. El base de 28 años y 1,85 m, que fue campeón de la NBA en 2024 y Sexto Hombre del Año en 2025, consigue una extensión máxima totalmente garantizada por dos años. La pasada temporada registró los mejores promedios de su carrera en puntos (17), asistencias (5,2) y rebotes (3,9). Pritchard, que actualmente juega bajo un contrato de 8 millones esta temporada y 8,3 millones el próximo año, percibirá más de 21 millones en la temporada 2028-29, antes de una opción mutua para la campaña 2029-30 valorada en casi 23 millones. La cadena ESPN destaca que Payton Pritchard es uno de los cuatro jugadores en la historia de los Celtics, junto con Tatum, Derrick White y Antoine Walker, que ha logrado anotar al menos 200 triples en múltiples temporadas. El de la Universidad de Oregon, que fue seleccionado por los Celtics con el número 26 del Draft de 2020, suma 241 partidos disputados en los últimos tres años que representan la tercera mayor cantidad de la NBA en ese periodo. Payton Pritchard tiene una conexión gallega desde su participación en Lugo en el campus infantil, el Campus Leyma Basquet English, al que acudió en 2010 y 2011. Entre los entrenadores que participaban en ese campus estaba Terry Pritchard, padre de Payton.

articles.title: In 2017, NBA star DeAndre Jordan raised $100,000 for Hurricane Harvey relief and donated 400 pairs of shoes to Houston students; years later, his generosity still inspires others to give back to their community
articles.summary: DeAndre Jordan was already making a name for himself in the NBA when Hurricane Harvey hit Texas in 2017.
articles.body: DeAndre Jordan was already making a name for himself in the NBA when Hurricane Harvey hit Texas in 2017. But the storm brought trouble to his hometown of Houston, and he wanted to help people dealing with its impact. The popular NBA center came up with a simple idea. He would use his rebounding skills to raise money for hurricane relief.Jordan's efforts did not end with the fundraising campaign. He also donated 400 pairs of shoes to students at a Houston elementary school. During his visit, he noticed that the school library needed more books and resources. That observation led to a reading club in 2018. Through these efforts, Jordan found different ways to support children in the city where he grew up.DeAndre Jordan used his NBA rebounds to support Hurricane Harvey reliefHurricane Harvey hit Texas in August 2017 and caused severe flooding across the Houston area. Many families faced damage to their homes and lost everyday belongings. The recovery would take time, and local communities needed help.For Jordan, the disaster affected a place he knew well. He grew up in Houston before attending Texas A&M University. The Clippers selected him with the 35th overall pick in the 2008 NBA Draft, and he went on to build a long career in the league.By 2017, Jordan had become known for his rebounding and defensive work. He had also earned his first NBA All-Star selection earlier that year. He decided to connect that part of his game with a fundraising effort for people affected by the hurricane.Through his Rebounds to Rebuild campaign, Jordan pledged to donate $100 for every rebound he collected during the 2017-18 NBA season. He also set a minimum commitment of $100,000 for Harvey relief.The idea gave his work on the basketball court a purpose beyond the game. Every rebound could help raise money for families dealing with the aftermath of the storm.Jordan's Treehouse Giving Foundation reports that the campaign raised more than $100,000 for hurricane relief. The figure reflects the amount raised through the initiative, rather than a claim that Jordan personally donated exactly that sum.The campaign was one way for Jordan to support Houston from a distance while continuing his NBA season. But he also wanted to help children directly.That brought him to Thompson Elementary School in Houston. He visited the school with his mother, Kim, in 2017. The visit led to a donation that students could use in their everyday lives.DeAndre Jordan donated 400 pairs of shoes to Houston studentsJordan visited Thompson Elementary School after Hurricane Harvey and donated 400 pairs of shoes to students through Shoes That Fit, a programme that provides footwear to children in need.For families recovering from a natural disaster, replacing everyday items can be difficult. Children still need shoes for school, and parents may have to manage these expenses while dealing with damage to their homes.The donation gave students something practical they could use. It also gave them a chance to meet an NBA player who had grown up in their city.One student shared their reaction to receiving the shoes. “My new shoes make me feel amazing in a happy way. It’s a great feeling!” the student said, according to Jordan's foundation.Another student, Jamari Ferrias, also spoke about the visit. “The visit meant so much more than a new pair of shoes,” Ferrias said. He explained that meeting Jordan made him feel as though the world had come to him and that he could be famous too.The comments show how much the visit meant to the students. Jordan had come to their school to help, but he also gave them the chance to meet someone they knew from basketball.During the visit, Jordan and his mother noticed another need. The school library lacked books and resources, and they wanted to help students get better access to reading material.The discovery led to another project at Thompson Elementary School. This time, the focus was on encouraging children to read.His school visit inspired a reading club in 2018Jordan's visit to Thompson Elementary helped inspire Ms. Kim's Timeout for Reading Book Club, which launched in March 2018. His mother, Kim, played an important role in the initiative, which aimed to encourage students to read more often.The programme supported improvements to the school's library and gave students a way to track their reading. It also offered incentives for children who completed books during the year.The idea was straightforward. Students needed access to books, but they also needed encouragement to keep reading. The club aimed to make reading a regular part of their school experience.Tanya Edwards, the school's principal, spoke about the programme in a statement published by Jordan's foundation.“The Timeout to Read event has Thompson’s students excited about reading!” Edwards said. She explained that students were reading the books provided through the initiative and recording their reading time.The programme gave Jordan's visit another purpose. The shoe donation helped provide an everyday essential, while the reading club focused on books and learning. Both efforts grew out of his connection with the school and its students.The foundation documents the club's launch and the school's early response. However, there is no verified information in these records confirming that the programme still operates today. Its lasting impact should not be overstated.Jordan's work in Houston was also part of a wider effort to support children and families. His Treehouse Giving Foundation organised DJ's 6 Days of Giving in 2017. The programme included a shopping trip for 100 children, a donation of 600 colouring books and teddy bears to patients at Children's Hospital Los Angeles, and an outing for six Houston families affected by Hurricane Harvey to attend a Clippers game.These activities supported children in different ways. Some provided useful items, while others gave families an opportunity to enjoy an experience during a difficult period.Jordan's efforts after Hurricane Harvey brought together fundraising and direct community support. He pledged money for relief, donated shoes to students and helped inspire a school reading club.His NBA career gave him a platform, but his connection to Houston gave these efforts a personal side. The city was where he grew up, and helping its children allowed him to give something back.Jordan could not undo the damage caused by Hurricane Harvey. But his fundraising campaign and work with Thompson Elementary provided practical support for people affected by the storm. His efforts also showed how an athlete can use his success to help children and families away from the basketball court.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Fantasy Basketball 2026 Latest Rankings for Top NBA Players and Sleepers
articles.summary: Winning a fantasy basketball league title isn't easy.
articles.body:
Winning a fantasy basketball league title isn't easy.

Formulating a winning strategy sounds pretty simple, though, doesn't it?

You need stars, obviously, and then you need to surround them with solid support pieces and the right amount of sleepers. Throw in copious amounts of good health, and you may have just created a championship recipe.

The execution doesn't always work the way the on-paper calculations say it should, and the injury bug doesn't always cooperate.

But those are concerns for a different day. For now, with optimism all the way up during the NBA preseason, we can dare to dream about what could happen if everything breaks right, so let's prepare for that surely-coming-to-fruition title run ahead with player rankings and a couple of our favorite sleeper picks.

Sleeper: Ajay Mitchell, PG/SG, Oklahoma City Thunder

What makes a good sleeper? Well, players can't have a high draft cost, obviously. Ideally, they have a track record showing some intriguing per-minute production. And maybe they're looking at an increased role that could push them to previously unseen statistical heights.

Ajay Mitchell checks all of those boxes.

He shouldn't cost you a top 100 pick. He just averaged 18.9 points, 5.0 assists and 2.1 stocks per 36 minutes last season, while shooting 48.5 percent overall and 87 percent at the line. His floor time should be trending up after OKC subtracted Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe this offseason.

Mitchell has legitimate breakout potential, but he just happens to be available at a sleeper draft price. Between his efficiency, scoring and two-way playmaking, he could be a fantasy asset.

Quentin Grimes, SG/SF, Los Angeles Lakers

Quentin Grimes seems a near certainty to start for a Lakers team that should field one of the league's best offenses. He quietly has a fairly compelling case to serve as their third option, too.

His offensive punch is quietly pretty powerful. Despite handling a reserve role the past two seasons, he still averaged more than 13 points with three-plus assists. He also shot a solid 45.9 percent from the field and an even 80 percent at the line.

He could be more efficient than ever while playing off of gravitational forces like Luka Dončić (whom Grimes played with in Dallas) and Austin Reaves. Grimes, a 38-plus-percent three-point shooter in three of his five NBA seasons, could feast on clean looks this season. And he'll have opportunities to create offense when teams inevitably sell out on stopping the Lakers' guards.

Grimes can also be helpful in steals and relatively useful on the glass. He should touch enough stat categories to return real value on what should be a middling (at most) draft price.

articles.title: Markus Howard sale del Baskonia rumbo al Zenit San Petersburgo
articles.standfirst: Se desvincula del club vitoriano tras más de cuatro temporadas como azulgrana y jugará en Rusia a las órdenes de Dusko Ivanovic, con quien brilló en la Euroliga
articles.summary: Se desvincula del club vitoriano tras más de cuatro temporadas como azulgrana y jugará en Rusia a las órdenes de Dusko Ivanovic, con quien brilló en la Euroliga
articles.body: El Kosner Baskonia confirmó este miércoles la salida del club de Markus Howard, que jugará en el Zenit de San Petersburgo, a las órdenes de Dusko Ivanovic, con quien brilló en la Euroliga. El jugador estadounidense se desvincula del club vitoriano tras más de cuatro temporadas como azulgrana y después de levantar el título de campeón de la Copa del Rey el curso pasado. Markus Howard llegó a la capital alavesa en el verano de 2022. Desde entonces ha defendido la camiseta azulgrana en un total de 244 partidos oficiales entre Euroliga (130), Liga Endesa (109), Copa del Rey y Supercopa (5) y ha sido uno de los capitanes baskonistas durante las últimas dos temporadas. El jugador estadounidense fue el máximo anotador de la Euroliga y de la liga ACB en la temporada 2023-24 y deja el Baskonia como segundo máximo triplista en la historia del equipo en la Liga Endesa, solo por detrás de Mirza Teletovic, y como el jugador con más triples anotados en una única temporada en la historia de la competición continental. Tras dos primeras temporadas excelentes, cambia de aires tras dos años en los que sus guarismos bajaron notablemente, aunque continuó dejando destellos de su calidad. "Compromiso y carácter Baskonia de un jugador que se marcha de Vitoria-Gasteiz tras haber logrado un legado como azulgrana. El nombre de Markus Howard está escrito ya para siempre en los libros de historia de este club, que siempre le recordará con cariño y que le desea la mejor de las suertes en su futuro personal y profesional", apuntó el club en su nota de prensa de despedida.

articles.title: Bronny James Called Out by Lakers HC JJ Redick amid Struggles in NBA Preseason
articles.summary: Los Angeles Lakers guard Bronny James drew a somewhat critical assessment from coach JJ Redick following Tuesday's 101-89 NBA preseason loss to the Golden State Warriors.
articles.body:
Los Angeles Lakers guard Bronny James drew a somewhat critical assessment from coach JJ Redick following Tuesday's 101-89 NBA preseason loss to the Golden State Warriors.

"I thought he had a really nice September and a good summer with us," Redick told reporters in his postgame press conference. "I don't think he's played well in the four preseason games, but he's had good practices. Some of it's just rhythm. Some of it's who he's playing with. He's played a lot of minutes, especially in the second half of games, with our two-way guys."

James appeared in each of the Lakers' first four preseason games. In 17.5 minutes per contest, he has averaged 2.8 points on 26.7 percent shooting along with 3.3 assists and 0.5 steals.

It's a limited sample, and preseason games are mostly about getting everyone up to speed physically. Still, James shooting sub-30 percent isn't an encouraging sign.

The 22-year-old is entering what's likely to be an important season for his tenure in Los Angeles. He has a team option for 2027-28, so he needs to show some improvement and demonstrate he can be an effective role player off the bench.

And much like the previous two years, James won't have a long runway to iron out his flaws on the court when the Lakers are chasing a title. Redick is going to lean on lineups that serve the team best right now.

Bronny will have one more opportunity to impress the coaching staff before the regular season tips off. The Lakers host the Denver Nuggets on Friday night.

articles.title: El Baskonia se carga a Galbiati: Perasovic, el recambio
articles.standfirst: El último puesto en la Euroliga pesó más que el liderato en la Liga Endesa y el entrenador croata iniciará una cuarta etapa en Vitoria
articles.summary: El último puesto en la Euroliga pesó más que el liderato en la Liga Endesa y el entrenador croata iniciará una cuarta etapa en Vitoria
articles.body: Paolo Galbiati ha dejado de ser entrenador del Kosner Baskonia. El entrenador italiano ya terminó cuestionado la temporada pasada y comenzó la actual de la misma manera. Sin embargo, el club baskonista decidió una continuidad que ha mantenido pendiendo de un hilo hasta ahora. Tras confirmar oficialmente su salida, su recambio en el banquillo del Buesa Arena sería Velimir Perasovic, cuyo nombre hace meses que se veía escuchando por Vitoria. El Baskonia vivía actualmente una situación contradictoria. Es el actual colista de la Euroliga con un balance de 1-4 después de las cinco primeras jornadas con cuatro de ellas jugadas en casa, pero es líder de la Liga Endesa con 3-0 y +61 de average por delante del Real Madrid y el Río Breogán, los otros dos invictos. El peso de Europa es mucho mayor en la balanza. Esa única victoria ante el Armani Milan, otro de los equipos de abajo, y la débil defensa mostrada han terminado costándole el cargo a Galbiati, que es el primer entrenador destituido esta temporada en la Euroliga. Este viernes, los vitorianos visitan a la Virtus. El entrenador italiano tenía una especial conexión con la grada del Buesa y con el vestuario. El título de Copa del Rey conseguido la temporada pasada reforzó ese vínculo. Se trataba de la primera Copa del Baskonia desde 2009 y de su primer éxito desde la Liga Endesa de la burbuja organizada en Valencia por el COVID. Galbiati ya había estado a punto de ser despedido antes de aquella conquista. "Soy un superviviente", dijo tras ganar. En verano, su marcha pareció hecha. Era el entrenador deseado por el Barcelona para suplir a Xavi Pascual, pero la operación no fructificó. El Baskonia no le quería, pero sí intentó rascar una indemnización. Cuando en el Palau se decidieron por fichar a Aleksander Sekulic, los vitorianos se vieron forzados a quedarse con un técnico que no les convencía. Y de ahí también la mala planificación en verano, viendo ir a jugadores, sobre todo interiores, y tardando en hacer fichajes. Se marcharon Mamadi Diakite (Dubai Basketball) y Khalifa Diop (Cavaliers) y llegó Kenneth Faried, que con 2,03 metros y 35 años debería ser un complemento, no un titular. Aterrizó Alex Len, pero llegó lesionado. Hace poco se ha fichado al brasileño Marcio Santos y ahora se busca otro interior. Christian Koloko es el deseado, pero su incorporación parece improbable. En esas aguas ha tenido que navegar Galbiati en este inicio de curso. Ahora se confirma su marcha, el despido más prematuro en una campaña del Baskonia. El récord lo tenía Joan Peñarroya, al que se le rescindió el contrato a finales de octubre de 2023 en una situación semejante: cuestionado en verano, continuó y se le cortó al poco de empezar la temporada. Entonces, el recambio fue Dusko Ivanovic. Ahora volverá otro clásico: Velimir Perasovic. El entrenador croata se liberó de su contrato en el UNICS Kazan ruso y empezará su cuarta etapa en Vitoria.

articles.title: Olivia Miles, Azzi Fudd, Flau'jae Johnson Headline 2026 WNBA All-Rookie Team
articles.summary: The Minnesota Lynx's Olivia Miles and Dallas Wings' Azzi Fudd led the way for the WNBA's 2026 All-Rookie team.
articles.body:
The Minnesota Lynx's Olivia Miles and Dallas Wings' Azzi Fudd led the way for the WNBA's 2026 All-Rookie team.

Chicago Sky guard Sydney Taylor, Seattle Storm guard Flau'jae Johnson, New York Liberty guard Pauline Astier and Toronto Tempo guard Kiki Rice rounded out the list of honorees.

Miles had a rookie season for the record books, surpassing Caitlin Clark's mark for the most points by a first-year player.

The 5'10" playmaker averaged 19.8 points, 4.7 rebounds, 6.0 assists and 1.3 steals. She was also an efficient scorer, shooting 49.2 percent overall and 38.8 percent from beyond the arc.

Miles' biggest achievement is the leadership and poise she displayed while the Lynx were waiting for Napheesa Collier to return from ankle surgery. Minnesota hardly missed a beat despite missing the five-time All-Star. Rookies typically don't impact winning in the way Miles did.

As the No. 1 pick in the 2026 draft, Fudd will have the misfortune of being intertwined with Miles for the duration of her career. Her production was contrasted with that of the player who went second overall in April.

Fudd averaged 13.1 points and shot 39.7 percent from the perimeter. Her season came to a premature end thanks to knee surgery, which played into one of the bigger concerns about her long-term outlook.

When healthy, Fudd at least displayed the shooting prowess that will help her carve out a productive career.

The Storm fully embraced their rebuild status, finishing with the WNBA's worst record (8-36). Johnson and fellow rookie Awa Fam at least helped to provide some excitement about the organization's future.

Johnson averaged 14.9 points and 2.9 assists. She had three double-doubles and finished with a season-high 29 points in a September loss to the Las Vegas Aces.

Taylor was similarly a bright spot in a frustrating season for the Sky. The 25-year-old also served as a success story for college standouts who don't immediately find a place in the WNBA.

After playing two years overseas, Taylor signed a training camp contract with Chicago. She earned a spot on the opening-night roster and eventually assuming a bigger scoring burden than expected with Skylar Diggins and Rickea Jackson out injured. In 37 games, she averaged 13.6 points.

Miles figures to cast a big shadow over her peers in the 2026 class. Over time, she shouldn't be the only star to emerge from this past draft.

articles.title: Olivia Miles, Azzi Fudd, Flau'jae Johnson headline WNBA All-Rookie team
articles.summary: The All-Rookie team features the top two picks in the 2026 draft in Fudd and Miles as well as two players who joined the league as undrafted free agents in S...
articles.body:
Rookie of the Year Olivia Miles leads a WNBA All-Rookie team that also features Azzi Fudd, Flau'jae Johnson, Pauline Astier, Kiki Rice and Sidney Taylor.

The WNBA announced the All-Rookie team on Wednesday. It features the top two picks in the 2026 draft in Fudd and Miles as well as two players who joined the league as undrafted free agents in Taylor and Astier.

Miles, the No. 2 pick of the draft out of TCU, took the league by storm. She earned first-team All-WNBA honors as the leader in points and assists for a Minnesota Lynx team that finished with the best record in the league before a disappointing first-round exit in the playoffs.

Miles averaged 19.8 points, 6 assists, 4.7 rebounds and 1.3 steals per game while shooting 49.2% from the floor and 38.8% from 3. Her 790 points broke the WNBA's record for points by a rookie.

Fudd, the No. 1 pick out of UConn, delivered in her first season with the Dallas Wings as a two-way player and one of the league's top 3-point threats. She averaged 13.1 points, 1.7 steals and 0.8 blocks while shooting 39.7% on 5.2 3-point attempts per game for a Wings team that earned the No. 7 seed in the playoffs. A knee injury cut her rookie season short at 30 games.

Johnson joined the the Seattle Storm as the No. 8 pick after an All-America career at LSU. She finished second in scoring among rookies and for the Storm while averaging 14.9 points, 4.8 rebounds, 2.9 assists and 1.4 steals per game

Rice joined the fledgling Toronto Tempo as the No. 6 pick in the draft after winning an NCAA championship with UCLA. She finished third in scoring and assists for the Tempo while averaging 13.4 points and 3.5 assists per game.

Astier joined the Liberty as an undrafted free agent out of France and started for a New York team that advanced to the second round of the playoffs. She averaged 9.3 points, 3.3 assists and 2.7 rebounds per game.

Taylor also earned a starting job after signing as an undrafted free agent. She averaged 13.6 points, 2 assists and 1.7 rebounds per game for the Chicago Sky.

articles.title: NBA Preview 2026-27: Reintroduction to the top 9 title contenders
articles.summary: Let's get reacclimated with the NBA's expected upper echelon by considering the cases for and against each team.
articles.body:
Since we last experienced NBA basketball games that count, we have seen:

34 trades involving more than 90 players, including 11 All-Stars, plus a frankly ludicrous number of future draft picks;

An estimated $2.5 billion in contracts signed in free agency ;

21 extensions of existing contracts totaling an additional $1.8 billion, headlined by Victor Wembanyama's five-year, $255 million not- quite -supermax ;

The Los Angeles Clippers receiving the stiffest punishment in NBA history ; and

The leading scorer in NBA history choosing to go to — and commute to — Philadelphia.

That's a ton of business to sift through as we get set for the start of the 2026-27 NBA season, and try to do some back-of-the-envelope math on which teams we expect to find — and expect to find themselves — in championship contention come June. So, as I've done at the start of each of the last five seasons , with all of our hopes still high for the potential outcomes of all those just-signed deals and newly consummated trades, unsullied by high-velocity contact with the brick wall of reality: Let's get to siftin'.

According to BetMGM , nine teams enter this season with championship odds of 25-to-1 (+2500) or better. Those nine teams feature 10 of the 15 members of last season's All-NBA teams … and they also feature major questions that must be answered between now and the postseason.

Let's get reacclimated with the NBA's expected upper echelon by considering the cases for and against those top nine teams, beginning with a team looking to bounce back after falling short of a bid for a championship repeat:

The case for: They have the league's two-time reigning Most Valuable Player in Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, which is a pretty good place to start. Also, they went the distance with Wemby and Co. in the Western Conference finals — a two-possession game in the final two minutes — despite their second- and third-best offensive creators, All-NBA wing Jalen Williams and breakout guard Ajay Mitchell, missing time with injuries over the course of the series.

Those guys are back and healthy, which should help Oklahoma City maintain the effectiveness of a group that has finished in the top six in offensive efficiency three years running . Isaiah Hartenstein and Chet Holmgren return to backstop the NBA's best defense — a unit that allowed nine fewer points per 100 possessions than league average last season, which is the largest differential in 30 years, according to PBP Stats .

The Thunder don't boast quite the same level of continuity that they had heading into last year, after trading away longtime point-of-attack linchpin Luguentz Dort, sharpshooting guard Isaiah Joe and reserve swingman Aaron Wiggins to chop down their luxury tax bill . But with All-Defensive selection Cason Wallace ready to step into an even larger role in Dort's stead, Mitchell joining Alex Caruso and Jared McCain in what's still a talented reserve corps in the backcourt, and a slew of other recent draftees looking to compete for minutes — including rookies Aday Mara and Bennett Stirtz, who've looked impressive in preseason action — the Thunder still have the potential to be one of the league's deepest teams.

Oklahoma City finished with the West's No. 1 seed and the league's best net rating last season despite Gilgeous-Alexander, Williams, Hartenstein and Mitchell combining to miss 123 games. Get a slightly cleaner bill of health — for J-Dub, in particular — and some development from the youngsters, and the Thunder could very well push for a third straight 60-plus win campaign and a real shot at hoisting the Larry O'Brien Championship Trophy once again.

The case against: As you might have heard, OKC struggles mightily with the Spurs , who beat the Thunder eight times in 12 tries last season and who don't appear to be going anywhere. Holmgren, in particular, seemed utterly bereft against Wembanyama in the Western finals; if he can't bounce back and find new answers to a particularly tall French problem that has plagued him since his prep days , the odds of Oklahoma City returning to the top of the mountain decline precipitously.

It's also possible that the Thunder's posited depth proves more theoretical than practical. If losing Dort, Wiggins and Joe requires more minutes for Caruso (whom OKC has essentially kept on a regular-season pitch count since his arrival) and veteran mainstay Kenrich Williams, will the Thunder's bench drop off? Mara and Stirtz look strong in preseason, but how effectively will they — or former lottery picks Nikola Topić and Thomas Sorber — translate to live action if pressed into duty against the likes of the Spurs?

I will grant that "can you get good minutes out of your ninth-through-14th guys" is the definition of a Champagne problem. When you've got championship expectations and you have to go through a monstrous opponent that has your number, though, all the pieces matter.

The case for: They return 98% of the postseason minutes from a team that finished in the top five in both offensive and defensive efficiency last season — one of just two NBA teams to do so, joining the Boston Celtics — and that went to the NBA Finals led by MVP finalist Wembanyama, who enters the season viewed by many as the ascendant best player in the world.

The Spurs went 35-7 — a 69-win pace — from mid-January through the start of the playoffs . They were dominant through the first two rounds of the postseason, and outclassed the defending champion Thunder, beating them in Oklahoma City in Games 1 and 7.

Yes, they came up short in the Finals, with the New York Knicks outscoring them by 26 points in fourth quarters , as they struggled with offensive execution and ball security, particularly in close-and-late situations. But they're already excellent, and the prospect of their most critical players — Wembanyama, Stephon Castle and rising sophomore Dylan Harper — actually getting better with another year of experience and development is downright frightening. (Ditto for forward Carter Bryant, a hyper-athletic defensive monster with the tools to carve out a bigger role in Year 2.)

If the youngsters grow from their defeat, if De'Aaron Fox can play more like the steady set of hands that earned an All-Star nod than the injured-and-shaky version that disappointed in the Finals , and if incoming vet Tobias Harris can add another reliable two-way frontcourt presence alongside Sixth Man of the Year Keldon Johnson, the re-signed Julian Champagnie and Harrison Barnes, then San Antonio could have everything it needs to not only make another run at a ring, but finish the job this time.

The case against: Progress isn't always linear. It's possible that, despite their arrows all seemingly trending straight up, Wembanyama, Castle, Harper and the rest of the Spurs' bright young things hit more developmental speed bumps this season than they did last year.

Maybe leaning harder into three-guard alignments to more frequently feature Harper upsets the lineup balance that head coach Mitch Johnson found over the course of the Finals run. Maybe Fox struggles to get past his frustrating Finals, and the already loud rumblings over whether Harper should start in his place grow deafening.

Or, y'know, maybe things go swimmingly, and the Spurs just find themselves on the short end of the stick this time against a Thunder team that projects as at least their equal. Getting to within arm's reach of the brass ring is hard; staying there is even harder.

The case for: A team that won 45 games and made it to the second round of the playoffs added Jaylen Brown , an All-NBA two-way forward who finished sixth in MVP voting last season, and LeBron James, who was the best player on a team that won a Western Conference playoff series six months ago and who should be precisely the kind of connective playmaker who can help turn a talented roster into more than the sum of its parts.

James and Brown join former MVP Joel Embiid, All-NBA point guard Tyrese Maxey and Rookie of the Year finalist VJ Edgecombe in a lineup that just might be the most talented starting five in the NBA. New arrivals Dean Wade, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope and Anfernee Simons bolster the second unit; first-round pick Labaron Philon Jr. adds some pop in the backcourt.

New general manager Mike Gansey has given head coach Nick Nurse plenty of toys to play with as he works to improve on last season's 17th-place finishes in offensive and defensive efficiency , to build on the Sixers' first playoff series win in three years, and to wash away the bitter taste of their second-round sweep at the hands of the eventual champion Knicks. Philly has its fair share of questions to answer; it also has every reason to harbor real hopes about its chances of breaking through the second-round ceiling and, at long last, legitimately competing for a championship.

The case against: It starts, as ever, with the health, availability and effectiveness of Embiid, who has played just 109 total regular-season and playoff games over the last three seasons. In that span, the Sixers have outscored opponents by 356 points with Embiid on the floor, and have been outscored by 729 points with him off it .

Backup center Ariel Hukporti is already lost for the season ; Adem Bona brings energy and rim protection, but isn't a big-minutes answer in the middle for a team with serious ambitions; small-ball looks with Wade, Dominick Barlow and LeBron at center run the risk of getting overwhelmed on the glass. For the Sixers to get where they want to go, the notably slimmed down Embiid has to stay upright and ambulatory — and prove better equipped to defend in space than he was against New York in Round 2 — in a way that we simply haven't seen from him deep into springtime.

Beyond Embiid, there's also the bit about the Sixers heavily relying on LeBron, who has played more minutes than anyone in NBA history and turns 42 in December, and skepticism in some quarters about how willingly and effectively Brown will operate in a context that will demand a dramatically reduced on-ball workload from what he enjoyed in Boston last season. If Nurse struggles to pull the right levers to get everyone their touches and put them all in position to succeed, the sheer talent on hand might not be enough to vault Philly to the top of the East, and ahead of their defending-champion rivals.

The case for: ICYMI: They just won the NBA championship , and put together arguably the most dominant single postseason run the sport's ever seen in the process.

New York returns the starting five that delivered the franchise's first championship in 53 years: Finals Most Valuable Player Jalen Brunson, the straw that stirs the drink ; center Karl-Anthony Towns, who played career-best ball on both ends of the floor during the title run; and top-flight wings OG Anunoby , Mikal Bridges and Josh Hart . Key bench guards Miles "Deuce" McBride, Landry Shamet, Jose Alvarado and Jordan Clarkson all return, too, while newcomer Andre Drummond gives head coach Mike Brown a veteran rebounding presence in the place of departed backup bigs Mitchell Robinson and Ariel Hukporti.

The Knicks entered the postseason as a very good team: 53 wins, a top-five offense, a top-10 defense, NBA Cup champions, with an elite clutch scoring option in Brunson. Between Game 3 against Atlanta and the final buzzer of Game 5 against San Antonio, though, they became a truly great team — a harmonic convergence of a roster that produced more than the sum of its already estimable parts, capable of playing splendid and damn near seamless basketball .

We've seen the Knicks lock into that rhythm and reach that rarefied air; we now know, beyond a shadow of a doubt, that they are capable of getting to that level. Who's to say they can't do it again?

The case against: No team has Done It Again since 2018, and only three teams since the Shaq-Kobe-Phil-era Lakers' millennium-opening threepeat have successfully run it back: the Kobe-Pau Lakers (2009, 2010), the Big Three Heat (2012, 2013) and the KD Warriors (2017, 2018). Getting everything to go right once is hard enough; going through consecutive seasons without something significant going awry seems damn near impossible in the modern NBA, as Tom Haberstroh and I discussed this summer on The Big Number:

It's not just that we haven't had a repeat titlist in eight years; no conference champion has even gotten back to the Finals after winning it all since the Warriors and Cavaliers renewed their annual unpleasantries from 2014 through 2018 (with the Warriors getting back in 2019, too).

On one hand, maybe the Knicks' utter dominance in the postseason — two sweeps, a five-game Finals, no series going the distance — means they won't be bringing the same wear-and-tear into the title defense as their predecessors. On the other, they have worn their fair share of tread off the tires: All five members of New York's starting five have played at least 6,000 minutes over the past two seasons, a heavy enough workload to make you wonder whether fatigue could wind up being a factor for Brown's main players.

Add in the potential significance of losing Robinson in free agency , the overall sour vibes surrounding the no-longer-ongoing negotiations on contract extensions for Towns, Hart and McBride , the way the East's depth and quality have risen around them, and the unavoidable challenge of going from the hunter to the hunted and having to face every opponent's best shot, and the Knicks enter ring night with their work cut out for them.

The case for: Coming off four straight seasons in which they'd won at least 50 games with three trips to the conference finals, two NBA Finals berths and one championship, Boston seemed poised to take a step back. Jayson Tatum was on the shelf after rupturing his Achilles tendon in the playoffs against the Knicks. Jrue Holiday, Al Horford and Kristaps Porziņġis were all gone, dealt in service of resetting the financial ledger; head coach Joe Mazzulla would now have to see what he could make out of half a championship rotation and a slew of unproven contributors.

What he made: a 56-win team that produced the NBA's second-best offense and fifth-best defense . Pretty good!

This year's model will be different from its predecessor, of course, remade by the stunning trade that sent Brown to Philly and imported Paul George — who has made it clear he's not trying to replace Brown , but whose higher-volume, higher-accuracy 3-point shooting and higher-end off-ball defensive work might make him a cleaner fit into the overarching possession-game-winning superstructure that Mazzulla, Brad Stevens and Co. have built at TD Garden.

Robinson comes in from the champs to fortify the frontcourt rotation alongside Neemias Queta. Mike Conley comes over from Minnesota to be the veteran sage in the room, bending the ears of ball-handlers Derrick White and the just-extended Payton Pritchard, young wings Baylor Scheierman, Hugo González and Jordan Walsh, and anyone else who might benefit from a little bit of hard-won wisdom at an opportune moment.

The pieces seem to fit. And if Tatum — who played less than 750 total minutes last season after his remarkable late-season return from Achilles rehab — is all the way back to his perennial All-NBA form as he steps into the central role that Brown occupied last season, it's easy to envision the Celtics cranking out another 50-plus-win campaign and entering the playoffs unafraid of any opponent they'll have to face.

The case against: Maybe Tatum, who missed the deciding Game 7 against the Sixers with left knee stiffness after his comeback, isn't all the way back to his perennial All-NBA form — or, at least, not enough to shoulder a superstar-level primary option workload.

Maybe George, who has played more than 56 games just once in the past seven years, and Robinson, who has logged just over 2,200 minutes over the last three seasons amid various lower leg injuries and load-management plans, aren't on the floor enough to make the kind of possession-tilting impact that Stevens envisions. Maybe White, fresh off the worst shooting season of his career, can't iron out the kinks on his jumper. And maybe, as overwhelming a mathematical advantage as Mazzullaball grants the Celtics over the broader 82-game sample, the spring once again finds them between a rock and a hard place if the jumpers stop falling and Boston doesn't have quite enough of a point-producing Plan B.

The case for: They bring back six of the nine guys who played at least 100 postseason minutes from a team that just made the Eastern Conference finals — the first time any Cavs team not featuring LeBron James has made it that far since 1992 — and swung a big trade that they hope will fill the hole they've had on the wing ever since their once and future King headed west to L.A.

The Cavs went 21-9 after the franchise-shifting trade of Darius Garland for James Harden , fielding the NBA's No. 4 offense in that span and outscoring opponents by nearly seven points per 100 possessions that Harden shared with All-NBA guard Donovan Mitchell. Their backcourt playmaking, combined with the defensive acumen of Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen, helped Cleveland grit its way through seven-game slugfests against the Toronto Raptors and Detroit Pistons to make it to a third-round showdown with the Knicks.

If not for blowing a 22-point lead in the fourth quarter of Game 1 , a chin-check from which they never fully seemed to recover, they might've been the ones staring down Wemby in June. Alas.

Rather than look to tear the foundation asunder after such a demoralizing defeat, the Cavs held firm: a massive extension for Mitchell , an attempt to reunite with LeBron, an eventual re-up for Harden , no mammoth tear-down swaps of Mobley or Allen. Instead, Cleveland shuffled the deck on the wing, taking part in a five-team, six-player, multi-pick sign-and-trade to land Peyton Watson, and subsequently sign the former Denver Nuggets swingman to a four-year, $88 million contract extension to man the 3 spot between their All-Star guards and bigs. (Also: Mario Hezonja's here!)

It's a bet on Watson, who just turned 24, being able to both play a complementary role on both ends of the floor to plug Cleveland's gaps and eventually build on the strong stretch of scoring prowess he showed last season when the injury-plagued Nuggets put the ball in his hands and let him run with it. It's a bet that, with more reps together, the Mitchell-Harden partnership can reach an even higher ceiling, putting the Cavs in position to once again field a top-five-caliber offense. And it's a bet that, as ugly as that four-game sweep at the hands of the Knicks was, Cleveland's ongoing championship construction project — step by step, brick by brick, over the last half-decade — is closer to completion than its skeptics might think.

The case against: There's a reason those skeptics keep arching their eyebrows — the sense that, no matter how good the Cavs can look during the regular season or for any discrete set of possessions in the course of the postseason, they lack the kind of cohesion and collective oomph that can get a team through its dark night of the soul.

Maybe that's too facile an analysis. This team did survive Game 7 twice, after all, knocking out the No. 1 seed Pistons to advance to the third round, and the 6-foot-8 Watson provides the kind of length, athleticism and pop that Cleveland sorely lacked during the Knicks series. At this point, though, it doesn't seem wholly unreasonable to want to see this Cleveland core — Mitchell, Allen, Mobley and now Harden and Watson — prove that it can make it out of the East before you believe they've got the goods to do so.

The case for: The Raptors exited last season as a 46-win team with a top-seven defense and enough toughness and physicality to push the Cavs to Game 7 … but with an offense that too often profiled as rickety at best.

Toronto ranked in the top-10 in half-court offensive efficiency during the regular season , but that dropped to 16th against opponents with top-10 point differentials ; the Raps' 95.3 points-per-100 half-court mark in the playoffs would have ranked 25th during the regular season. They were 15th in clutch offensive efficiency during the regular season, and their playoff mark would've ranked 26th during the regular season. They've finished 22nd or lower in the total share of their shots that come from 3-point range in each of the last five seasons ; they made just 123 pull-up 3s en masse last season, dead last in the NBA by 46 triples.

All of which is to say: It's difficult to overstate just how perfectly Kawhi Leonard — who last season made 88 pull-up 3s by himself , led the NBA in points per touch , averaged a career-high 27.9 points per game on 51/39/89 shooting splits and was one of the most prolific fourth-quarter scorers in the league — fills the gaps in this team's résumé.

Importing an All-NBA offense-unto-himself reduces the playmaking and shot-creation burden on every other Raptor, which should result in Scottie Barnes, Immanuel Quickley, RJ Barrett and Co. having more space to operate, cleaner looks to cash out, and easier opportunities than they saw in an often congested half-court attack. And slotting in Leonard — who finished top-15 in the league in steals and deflections last season — should only further fortify Darko Rajaković's pressure-packing defense; the prospect of trying to probe for openings in lineups featuring Leonard, Barnes, rising sophomore Collin Murray-Boyles, Ja'Kobe Walter and the just-extended Jamal Shead is enough to induce claustrophobia in opposing perimeter players.

It's been understandably and justifiably obscured by the drama surrounding the investigation into salary-cap circumvention and his subsequent exit from L.A., but the version of Leonard we just saw was arguably one of the five or six best players in the entire NBA last season. If the Raptors get that version for 2,000 minutes — and, obviously and most crucially, get it into April, May and hopefully June — then this becomes a seriously dangerous outfit.

The case against: If they don't get that version — and here's where we remind ourselves that Kawhi has played 65 games just twice in the last nine years, hasn't finished a postseason healthy since 2020, and hasn't played more than two postseason rounds since the Raptors' 2019 title — then all that stuff goes up in smoke.

(More practically: If the Raptors wind up leaning into smaller-ball looks, with CMB replacing veteran Jakob Poeltl at the 5, will their rim protection and rebounding suffer against the best opponents? And even with Leonard stepping in for Brandon Ingram and Gradey Dick, is there still not quite enough shooting on this roster?)

We're about three and a half years removed from a team trading a bunch of draft capital for a 34-year-old All-NBA forward with the expectation that it would help vault them into the upper reaches of contention; the Kevin Durant era in Phoenix didn't work out so hot. Maybe, due to the presence of Barnes and the picks they've still got access to, the Raptors are better positioned to weather such a disappointment without cratering. But getting Kawhi at a bargain price doesn't mean there's no downside risk of relying on him to get where you want to go.

The case for: They still have Nikola Jokić, and you still don't.

Even with Jokić, Aaron Gordon, Christian Braun, Cameron Johnson and Peyton Watson combining to miss 129 games, Denver still fielded by far the NBA's No. 1 offense and won 54 games last season. The Nuggets annihilated opponents by 18.8 points-per-100 with Jokić, Murray and Gordon all on the floor last season; the framework of what's made this team work at such a high level for the better part of a decade is still here. Get healthier seasons from Gordon and Johnson, a bounce-back from Braun — who shot just 30.1% from 3-point range last season after knocking 'em down at a 38.4% clip over his first three years — and just a sprinkling of production from someone off the bench (DeMar DeRozan? Tyus Jones? Marvin Bagley?) and nobody's going to want to see this offense come springtime.

The case against: They will , however, probably be excited to see a Denver defense that has finished 21st in points allowed per possession in each of the last two seasons . The Nuggets don't force turnovers, don't protect the rim and really don't stop opponents on the fast break; they've allowed more than 1.3 points per play in transition in each of the last two seasons, bottom-two marks in the league.

If that doesn't improve dramatically, the Nuggets' chances of winning three playoff series — already complicated by the presence of Oklahoma City and San Antonio, and by the drip-by-drip defections of depth since their 2023 title run — are likely somewhere between slim and none. And if the 31-year-old Gordon, who has missed 77 games over the past two seasons and been hampered by recurring hamstring injuries in consecutive playoff runs, can't stay upright and on the floor, "slim" may have already left town.

The case for: After making consecutive trips to the Western Conference finals, the Timberwolves took down the Nuggets and pushed the Spurs to six with Anthony Edwards hobbled, Ayo Dosunmu limited, Donte DiVincenzo sidelined and precious little point guard play to speak of. Well, they've got a point guard now. And he likes to go fast.

The theory of the case: The arrival of LaMelo Ball to pair with Anthony Edwards cranks up the offensive variance in Minnesota to a senses-shattering degree, affording the Wolves the opportunity to explore new frontiers in pull-up 3-point shooting volume and geometry warping on offense. Force the defense to cover more ground and you open up more driving lanes and opportunities to feast on the inside. Hunt early offense with LaMelo's penchant for hit-aheads and half-court lobs to the likes of Edwards, Jaden McDaniels and newcomer Jonathan Kuminga, and a Minnesota offense that has largely lagged behind its elite Rudy Gobert-helmed defense might finally catch up — a stylistic pivot that could make the Wolves considerably more formidable, and give them a hell of a puncher's chance, against Oklahoma City and San Antonio in a best-of-seven.

The case against: It starts, as these so often do, with health. Ball played 72 games and 2,017 minutes last season, recurring ankle issues led him to average 35 appearances and 1,161 minutes over the previous three; if he can't stay healthy, he can't supercharge the offense in the ways Tim Connelly and Co. are hoping.

It remains to be seen how effectively head coach Chris Finch can maintain an elite defense around Ball. And how comfortably LaMelo can shoulder the quantum leap in operational duties required of the primary ball-handler and table-setter of a team that harbors legitimate championship aspirations. And how neatly Kuminga, once again singing for his supper after taking a bargain-bin deal on a team that likely needs him to fit in (read: defense, rebounding, screening, running the floor) more than stand out (read: hunt isos, try to score 20). And how the defense holds up when the 34-year-old Gobert — quietly one of the most interesting potential free agents in the league right now — takes a rest. And how a second unit that's now heavily dependent on both Dosunmu maintaining his level of play and leaps from second-year center Joan Beringer and Terrence Shannon Jr. holds up against the best of the best.

That's a lot of questions. They're different ones, though — and, for a team looking to zag in pursuit of a new angle of attack against the conference's top flight, maybe that's enough for now.

Hey, here's a fun fact: I've written this column five times, and each year, at least one eventual NBA Finals participant was not included in it!

Last year , the Spurs didn't make the cut. The year before that , the Indiana Pacers didn't. The 2023 edition didn't include the Dallas Mavericks. The 2022 version didn't feature either the Nuggets or Miami Heat. And the first go-round, back in 2021 , didn't have the Celtics on it.

Which is to say: We're almost guaranteed to see someone that you didn't just read about playing for the Larry O'B come June! (That's how probability works, right?)

The teams that didn't come in under +2500, but that bear monitoring in the big picture, include:

Detroit Pistons (+3000): Yes, the Jalen Duren drama was taxing, and yes, I have my questions about the net outcome of effectively swapping Tobias Harris for John Collins. But the Pistons added shooting (Collins, Isaiah Joe, Taurean Prince) to the core of a team that won 60 games, finished with the East's No. 1 seed, came within one game of the Eastern Conference finals, and absolutely hammered the eventual champion Knicks during the regular season with Cade Cunningham at the controls. Maybe we shouldn't be too quick to overlook them?

Miami Heat (+3000): Hey, remember these guys? They finished above .500 and just outside the top 10 on both ends of the floor last season, and they just traded for Giannis Antetokounmpo — one of the few players who can at any given point lay legitimate claim to being the best player on the planet. If he's able to play closer to 70 games than the 36 he managed last season, and if Erik Spoelstra's able to find the right balance between bully-ball and pace-and-space lineup combinations, the Giannis-Bam Adebayo partnership could be lethal .

Los Angeles Lakers (+3500): The last time Luka Dončić had a properly built team around him — screen-and-dive rim-protecting center, high-efficiency secondary scorers and playmakers, active 3-and-D wings — he went to the NBA Finals . Now he's got Walker Kessler, Austin Reaves, Quentin Grimes, Matisse Thybulle, Ziaire Williams and Collin Sexton. Maybe that's not enough to put the fear of God into OKC and San Antonio. But maybe it is.

Indiana Pacers (+4000): The last time we saw Tyrese Haliburton healthy, he had the Thunder on the ropes in Game 7 in their own gym. I can't blame anyone who wants to pump the brakes on the Pacers getting back to that level. But I also don't have too hard a time seeing Indiana — now with Ivica Zubac to join the rest of that Finals core — hitting the gas to return to what it views as its rightful perch.

Houston Rockets (+5000): A 52-win team that finished top-seven on both ends of the floor gets back the organizing-principle point guard (Fred VanVleet) that it missed for all of last season and the goliath offensive-rebounding center (Steven Adams) who helped form its ground-and-pound point-scoring identity, and adds a tough-as-nails veteran defender (Marcus Smart) who should be a perfect fit for the postseason pressure cooker. Oh, and they still have Kevin Durant, who just averaged 26 a night on 52/41/87 shooting, and a handful of 25-and-under dudes — Alperen Şengün, Amen Thompson, Jabari Smith Jr., Reed Sheppard, Tari Eason — who all still have the potential to take another step forward in their development. This team's floor is really high; if a couple of things break right, its ceiling could be championship-caliber.

articles.title: LeBron James Explains Why He Thinks OG Anunoby Was Knicks' NBA Finals MVP Over Jalen Brunson
articles.summary: Philadelphia 76ers forward LeBron James believes forward OG Anunoby was the New York Knicks' MVP in last season's Finals, per comments made on his Mind the Game podcast with Steve Nash amid a 2026-27 season preview (5:20 mark).
articles.body:
Philadelphia 76ers forward LeBron James believes forward OG Anunoby was the New York Knicks' MVP in last season's Finals, per comments made on his Mind the Game podcast with Steve Nash amid a 2026-27 season preview (5:20 mark).

Anunoby averaged 21.2 points on 52.5 percent shooting, 4.8 rebounds, 1.4 blocks and 1.4 steals in five NBA Finals games against the San Antonio Spurs. His game-winning tip-in in Game 4 to complete a 29-point comeback in a 107-106 victory is one of the more iconic NBA moments in recent memory.

He was incredible all game, though, finishing with 33 points and providing great defense, including a game-saving block on Spurs point guard De'Aaron Fox on the previous possession.

Knicks captain and guard Jalen Brunson ended up winning NBA Finals MVP, and that award certainly made sense given that he averaged a series-high 32.6 points per game. That included a 45-point effort in the series-closing Game 5, which the Knicks won 94-90.

However, Anunoby was sensational as well and did all the little things, as James noted.

James and the 76ers will visit the Knicks to open their regular season on Tuesday, Oct. 20.

articles.title: Clippers Make Another Surprising Roster Decision With Regular Season Looming
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Clippers waived third-year guard and 2024 second-round pick Cam Christie on Wednesday, per ESPN's Shams Charania. The post Clippers Make Anot...
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Clippers waived third-year guard and 2024 second-round pick Cam Christie on Wednesday, per ESPN's Shams Charania.

The Los Angeles Clippers are waiving guard 2024 second-round pick Cam Christie, sources tell ESPN. — Shams Charania (@ShamsCharania) October 14, 2026

The Los Angeles Clippers are waiving guard 2024 second-round pick Cam Christie, sources tell ESPN.

Shams Charania (@ShamsCharania) October 14, 2026

Christie, 21, featured in the majority of the Clippers' games last year after taking on a limited role in his rookie season in 2024-25, but couldn't carve out a bigger role for the Clippers despite his increased involvement. Through his 55 games in 2025-26, Christie averaged just 2.8 points, 1.4 rebounds and 0.6 assists per game on just 8.7 minutes.

The brother of Dallas Mavericks guard and former Los Angeles Laker Max Christie, Cam had plenty of upside as a shooter entering the league after one year at Minnesota. He shot 39.1% from deep and averaged 11.3 points per game as a freshman in the Big Ten, earning an All-Freshman Team selection before declaring for the draft, but his skills are yet to translate in the NBA.

He has a career field goal percentage of just 36.8%, shooting just 22.6% from beyond the arc.

Christie featured heavily in each of the Clippers' two preseason games against the Warriors and Raptors, but failed to make much of a difference in either contest. He had eight points, eight rebounds and three assists against the Warriors on 2-of-8 shooting with five turnovers against the Warriors in 28 minutes, and had eight points and three rebounds in 21 minutes against the Raptors—though he was more efficient in that game, converting two of his three field goal attempts.

The Clippers also just cut guard Yuki Kawamura , as the guard positions are extremely crowded on their roster. In front of Christie, the Clippers had No. 5 overall pick Keaton Wagler, alongside Darius Garland, Gradey Dick, Max Strus and Kris Dunn. With so many players in front of him, Christie likely would have seen his role further reduced with the Clippers.

The Clippers still have the opportunity to keep Christie, as they still have a two-way spot open, though with guard Jalen Pickett already filling one of those spots, keeping Christie may be redundant.

Christie's best plan of action is to try his luck with other teams, but he has just a week to join a different organization before the 2026-27 NBA season begins.

articles.title: DeWine grants Ohio college athletes fifth year of eligibility
articles.summary: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine signed an executive order that gives a number of college athletes a fifth year of eligibility. The order, announced Tuesday, Oct. 13, i...
articles.body:
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine signed an executive order that gives a number of college athletes a fifth year of eligibility.

The order, announced Tuesday, Oct. 13, is the latest twist in a months-long saga that has created headlines in courtrooms around the country. The news came three weeks before the start of the 2026-27 college basketball season.

According to a press release, Executive Order 2026-04D "gives Ohio's public and private colleges and universities the option to allow all otherwise eligible student-athletes from the high school class of 2022 to compete despite the NCAA's current interpretation of its new eligibility rule."

Said DeWine, "When the rules change, fairness has to remain part of the equation. We want Ohio's student-athletes to have the same opportunity as student-athletes in other states."

While local college basketball programs such as Dayton, Miami and Wright State don't have players on the roster who will benefit from the order, their opponents do.

Dayton, for example, plays Cincinnati in November. One of Cincinnati's key players, if he's now eligible, will be Utah State transfer MJ Collins, who averaged 17.5 points per game last season.

The executive order does not appear to help former Dayton guard Javon Bennett because he's not on the roster of an Ohio team. He transferred to Gonzaga in the spring after playing one season at Merrimack and three at Dayton.

In June, Bennett was one of 15 Ohio college basketball players — all of whom started their careers in 2022 and played four seasons — who filed a lawsuit seeking an injunction against the NCAA's age-based eligibility model. The new rule allows athletes to play up to five seasons in five years but excludes athletes who exhausted their eligibility under the old rules in 2026.

The NCAA has fought the lawsuit — and others like it across the country — for months and will continue to do so, according to a statement by NCAA President Charlie Baker on Tuesday.

"The Governor of Ohio cannot legislate NCAA eligibility rules," Baker said. "One elected official seeking to make their own rules for their own schools' advantage is a terrible way to run athletic competitions and precisely why Congress must pass the PCSA as soon as possible.

"And not only did NCAA members vote unanimously to implement the age-based eligibility change in this way, the Ohio Court of Appeals just recently agreed with that decision.

"The Ohio Court of Appeals isn't alone in siding with the NCAA on this issue as multiple appellate courts have now recognized the importance of consistent application of NCAA eligibility rules and the significant disruption that results when eligibility standards vary from institution to institution or state to state.

"The NCAA will protect the interests of all member institutions and student-athletes.

"Eligibility rules established through the Association's governance process have been and will continue to be applied consistently across the membership by the NCAA including in the state of Ohio."

articles.title: Red Wings interim GM Shawn Horcoff makes Simon Edvinsson trade declaration
articles.summary: The Detroit Red Wings took care of a critical piece of business this week, re-signing star forward Alex DeBrincat to a seven-year, $91 million contract exten...
articles.body:
The Detroit Red Wings took care of a critical piece of business this week, re-signing star forward Alex DeBrincat to a seven-year, $91 million contract extension.

Now, the spotlight returns to Dylan Larkin and Simon Edvinsson — and interim general manager Shawn Horcoff made his intentions clear on the latter on Wednesday afternoon.

"I have zero interest in trading Simon Edvinsson," Horcoff told reporters, including The Athletic's Max Bultman. "Not something I'm entertaining. We want to sign him."

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

After spending time in Sweden, Edvinsson headed back to North America this week, although his return does not necessarily signal a breakthrough in contract negotiations.

The 23-year-old emerged as one of Detroit's most important blueliners last season, recording 25 points in 72 games while assuming a top-four role. The former sixth overall selection in the 2021 NHL Draft played out the final season of his entry-level contract in 2025-26.

Edvinsson attended training camp without a new deal but eventually returned to Sweden as negotiations remained stalled.

The drama surrounding the Red Wings has continued to snowball after the team missed the Stanley Cup Playoffs for a 10th consecutive season in the spring — the longest active drought in the National Hockey League.

Larkin requested a trade shortly afterward, and Steve Yzerman has since stepped down as general manager.

When the 2026-27 season began with Edvinsson still unsigned, reports that he preferred a trade further complicated matters for Detroit's front office.

Now, with DeBrincat locked up long-term, Horcoff remains focused on reaching a contract agreement with the young Swede rather than moving him elsewhere.

The noise has been too much for the Wings to overcome in the early going. Detroit is 1-3-2 and last in the Atlantic Division through its first six games.

Where the franchise goes from here remains the big question, and it'll be interesting to see whether there is a resolution, one way or another, before the end of October.

The Red Wings are back in action Thursday night, hosting the winless Philadelphia Flyers at Little Caesars Arena.
